stem: A kidney recipient discharged last week calls the transplant coordinator only to confirm the date and time of an upcoming clinic visit. According to standard post-discharge communication teaching, how should this contact be classified?

options.text: An urgent matter requiring immediate evaluation for rejection
An urgent matter because all post-discharge calls must be triaged within 15 minutes
A matter that should be redirected to the emergency department without transplant team contact

explanation.rationale_correct: Verification of appointment date and time is explicitly listed among non-urgent reasons to contact the transplant team, distinct from urgent concerns such as infection, rejection symptoms, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

rationale_incorrect.B: Rejection-related symptoms are urgent matters; confirming a scheduled clinic time is not.
rationale_incorrect.C: References distinguish urgent from non-urgent contacts; not every call requires immediate rejection evaluation.
rationale_incorrect.D: Routine appointment verification should be handled through transplant team communication channels, not automatic ED referral.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → §h. Communication with the transplant team → ii. Non-urgent matters
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Verification of appointment date and time

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → §h. Communication with the transplant team → ii. Non-urgent matters (appointment verification); PDF p. 111 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Anchor verified against docs/reference/cupples-core-curriculum-2e.pdf p. 111.

stem: A coordinator is revising the post-discharge call guide for recipients and caregivers. Evaluate the following statements about when to contact the transplant team:

elements.text: Medication refill requests are examples of non-urgent matters.
Signs and symptoms of rejection are urgent matters.
General concerns about diet, activity, and exercise are urgent matters.
Shortness of breath is an urgent matter.

explanation.rationale_correct: Medication refills and similar routine needs are non-urgent, while rejection symptoms, infection concerns, chest pain, and shortness of breath require urgent outreach. General diet and activity questions are explicitly non-urgent.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also true—shortness of breath is listed as urgent.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement III is false; diet and exercise questions are non-urgent.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false; not all four statements are correct.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → §h. Communication with the transplant team → ii–iii (non-urgent vs urgent matters)
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Non-urgent matters may include Medication refills … Urgent matters may include Signs and symptoms of rejection … Shortness of breath

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → §h. Communication with the transplant team → ii. Non-urgent matters and iii. Urgent matters; PDF p. 111 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Synthesized item. Statements I–IV from Cupples Ch. 3 §h ii–iii; primary anchor on p. 111.

stem: When teaching a post-transplant recipient about immunosuppression, which statement should NOT be included in the teaching plan?

options.text: Transplant patients are more likely to become sick compared to non-transplant patients
Immunosuppressant doses may be taken at different times each day without concern
Notify the transplant coordinator if a new medicine is prescribed by the primary care doctor
Some foods and medications may change the metabolism of immunosuppressant drugs

explanation.rationale_correct: Standard immunosuppression teaching includes infection risk, drug–drug and drug–food interactions, and notifying the transplant team about new prescriptions. Taking immunosuppressants at inconsistent times each day is the exception—not appropriate teaching.

rationale_incorrect.A: Increased susceptibility to illness is part of standard immunosuppression education.
rationale_incorrect.C: Coordinators must be notified when outside prescribers add medications that may interact with transplant drugs.
rationale_incorrect.D: Food and medication interactions affecting immunosuppressant metabolism are taught routinely.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 4, Posttransplant Patient Education → immunosuppression teaching item 6 (EXCEPT)
primary_anchor.quote_hint: medication may be taken at different times each day

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 4 → posttransplant immunosuppression teaching (item 6: all included EXCEPT inconsistent dosing times); PDF p. 128 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Anchor verified against docs/reference/cupples-core-curriculum-2e.pdf p. 128.

stem: During post-transplant education for a liver recipient, which metabolic complication should the coordinator include as a condition that may be newly identified during the transplant phase?

options.text: Primary graft nonfunction diagnosed only at five years post-transplant
Permanent cure of pre-transplant type 1 diabetes without monitoring
Iron overload requiring immediate splenectomy in every recipient

explanation.rationale_correct: Post-transplant education includes that patients may be diagnosed with hyperglycemia or post-transplant diabetes during the transplant phase, warranting glucose monitoring and teaching.

rationale_incorrect.B: Primary nonfunction is an early graft event, not a metabolic diagnosis introduced at five years.
rationale_incorrect.C: Diabetes may persist or newly develop; immunosuppression does not guarantee permanent cure without monitoring.
rationale_incorrect.D: Splenectomy for iron overload is not a universal transplant-phase metabolic teaching point.
